meta.title: Who really said "Lead on, Macduff"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Shakespeare wrote “Lay on, Macduff” in Macbeth — a call to fight, not to lead the way. “Lead on, Macduff” is a famous folk misquotation.
meta.ogDescription: Shakespeare actually wrote “Lay on, Macduff” in Macbeth. “Lead on” is a centuries-old mishearing that reverses the meaning.

answer.label: Not Shakespeare’s words — a folk misquotation of Macbeth
answer.sourceLine: The line people mean is real, but the wording is not. In Macbeth (Act 5, Scene 8) Macbeth snarls “Lay on, Macduff, & damned be him that first cries ‘Hold! Enough!’” — a call to fight harder, not to lead the way. “Lead on, Macduff” is a centuries-old mishearing that flips the meaning into a polite ‘after you.’

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: MACBETH: I will not yield, / To kiss the ground before young Malcolm’s feet, / And to be baited with the rabble’s curse. … Yet I will try the last. Before my body / I throw my warlike shield. Lay on, Macduff, / And damned be him that first cries ‘Hold! Enough!’
trail: The Folger Shakespeare Library’s edition of Macbeth, Act 5, Scene 8 gives the line as “Lay on, Macduff, / And damned be him that first cries ‘Hold! Enough!’”
“Lay on” was an Elizabethan order to strike hard with a weapon; Macbeth and Macduff are sworn enemies mid-combat, so “lead on” makes no sense in context, as wordynerdbird’s explainer notes.
Word Histories traces the earliest documented “Lead on, Macduff” to the Lincolnshire Chronicle of 25 May 1855.
source.excerptNote: Macbeth’s defiant last words before his fatal duel — “lay on” meant ‘strike hard.’ He is challenging his enemy to fight, not asking to be led anywhere.

source.rightsNote: The genuine line is from Macbeth, first printed in the 1623 First Folio — long in the public domain. The popular wording “Lead on, Macduff” is a later folk corruption found in no Shakespearean text, so it has no separate authored source of its own.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare wrote Macbeth around 1606; it was first printed in the 1623 First Folio. The tragedy’s closing scene gives Macbeth his defiant battle-cry — the real line behind one of the most persistent Shakespeare misquotations in English.

copyAttribution: Shakespeare actually wrote "Lay on, Macduff, / And damned be him that first cries 'Hold! Enough!'" — Macbeth, Act 5, Scene 8 (First Folio, 1623). "Lead on, Macduff" is a later misquotation.

misattribution.heading: Right play, wrong word
misattribution.intro: “Lead on, Macduff” is real Shakespeare misremembered. The character and scene are genuine; the verb has been swapped, reversing what Macbeth actually means.

items.why: Shakespeare wrote “Lay on, Macduff” — an order to strike hard in combat. The everyday “Lead on, Macduff” turns a fight-to-the-death challenge into a polite ‘after you,’ a meaning Shakespeare never intended, per the Folger text.
The line does come from Macbeth (Act 5, Scene 8) — so the attribution to Shakespeare is not baseless; only the exact wording is wrong.

misattribution.truthLine: Shakespeare’s Macbeth says “Lay on, Macduff” — not “Lead on” — and the earliest documented “Lead on” version dates only to 1855, long after the play.

context.heading: Why the mix-up stuck
lead: The swap survives because it makes the phrase usable. “Lay on” is archaic combat slang; “lead on” is everyday English that fits any moment someone waves you ahead through a door. The mishearing is small — one consonant — but it converts a duel to the death into a courtesy.
In the play there is nothing polite about it: Macbeth, cornered and doomed, throws down his shield and dares Macduff to fight, cursing whoever yields first. That is the opposite of asking to be led.
context.pull: “Lay on” meant strike hard — not ‘after you.’
